title: How do you use the rule of 72 to estimate how long something takes to double?
description: The rule of 72: a quick way to do this case calculation in your head, with a worked example.
hook: The rule of 72 tells you how long it takes something to double. It is quick, accurate enough for any case, and impressive to use.
body:
The problem

A market grows 8% a year. How long to double?

Step by step

  1. Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate
  2. 72 ÷ 8

Answer: ≈ 9 years.

How to say it in the interview

A market grows eight percent a year. How long until it doubles?

Divide seventy two by the growth rate.

Seventy two divided by eight.

About nine years.

It works the other way too: to double in six years, you need about twelve percent a year.

Notice that the last step is always about meaning. A number on its own earns half the marks; a number with "so what" earns all of them.

Know the approximation's limits

At 8% growth, the rule gives roughly nine years to double. The more precise calculation is ln(2) ÷ ln(1.08), approximately 9.0 years. This is close because the rule of 72 works well for many common growth rates.

For a business shrinking at 8% annually, you cannot mechanically say "it halves in nine years" with the same accuracy. The compound decline factor is 0.92 each year, giving a half-life of ln(0.5) ÷ ln(0.92), about 8.3 years.

The rule is a speed tool, not a substitute for an exact model when a large investment depends on a narrow timing threshold.
